comments.text:
Considering over 100 million Americans are obese, this is probably a good thing. My weekly grocery for a single person is $50-$70/week. I have no idea what people are buying, but clearly I am not buying that. Oh, and nothing "packaged" - except for rice, beans, and the flour from which I bake bread weekly.  Food is affordable, however, "preferences" are expensive. Entitlement is the most expensive weekly expense a person can have. 

Here is a strategy:

Eat unprocessed/minimal processed food - no packaged snacks
Beans and rice are staples, not something for Tuesdays
Cut out things that are not nutritionally required
No restaurants
No fast food
No soda, no sugary drinks.
Make as much as you can yourself - bread, soups, snacks, casseroles, sauces, salads, dressings, tea or coffee, wine and beer (if you are into that and are of legal age) 
Buy at season peak - don't buy watermelon or asparagus in NYC in January. 
Learn to preserve, can, and ferment foods when they flood the market at rock bottom prices.
Get a $30 bidet on amazon and cut out 75% of your TP usage/cost (can pay for itself within a month for a family of 4)
Don't heat or cool your place when you are not home
Turn off lights
Cancel cable
Cancel cellphone plans other than what you NEED
Cancel subscriptions to entertainment (like Hulu or Netflix, or going to the "moovies"):  it's just brain washing anyway. 
Where possible walk, cycle, or car pool.  I cycle to work daily and the commute time is the same. This might not be possible for those who haul equipment or tools. 
Plant a garden of fast growing plants - herbs (expensive) can be grown for cheap. Fast tomato varieties like Early Girls can have a bushel of tomatoes ready in 90 days. Then can/freeze.
A frugal mindset does not mean poverty - it means intelligence. It is far easier to save than to make more.
If this doesn't sound like "fun" - that's the problem. Learn to like it.
